a136.speaker: United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR)
a136.name: United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR)
a136.speech: Is extremely concerned about the fate of thousands of Eritreans currently trapped between the two camps, as fighting intensifies in Tigray.

a136.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a136.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
a136.speech: Estimates that 3.8 million people in the region need emergency health assistance.

a136.speaker: Babar Balloch, spokesperson of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Geneva
a136.name: Babar Balloch
a136.title: spokesperson of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Geneva
a136.speech: Said around 24,000 Eritrean refugees, grouped in the camps of Mai Aini and Adi Harush near Mai Tsebri in Tigray, are currently victims of intimidation and harassment by unidentified armed groups.

a136.speaker: Information coming from Mai Aini (unattributed reports)
a136.name: Information coming from Mai Aini (unattributed reports)
a136.speech: According to information from Mai Aini, at least one refugee is reported to have been killed by armed elements operating inside the camp, a death that comes in addition to the murder of another refugee on 14 July.

a136.speaker: UNHCR (statement)
a136.name: UNHCR (statement)
a136.speech: “Implores all parties involved in the conflict to fulfil their obligations under international law, in particular by respecting the civilian character of refugee camps, the rights of refugees and of all civilians to be protected from hostilities.”

a136.speaker: David Beasley, head of the World Food Programme (WFP)
a136.name: David Beasley
a136.title: head of the World Food Programme (WFP)
a136.speech: Issued a cry of alarm so that the 170 trucks loaded with food and other essential items currently blocked can leave immediately, because by 30 July Tigray will have no more food.

a136.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a136.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
a136.speech: Acknowledges having extremely limited means in the Tigray region, so that hundreds of thousands of people, including victims of the fighting, pregnant women and survivors of sexual violence, have no access to basic care and essential medicines.

a136.speaker: Humanitarian agencies
a136.name: Humanitarian agencies
a136.speech: Are deeply concerned by the growing risk of severe acute malnutrition in Tigray.

a136.speaker: Ethiopian agency in charge of refugees (ARRA)
a136.name: Ethiopian agency in charge of refugees (ARRA)
a136.speech: According to ARRA, 92,000 Eritrean refugees lived in this region before the war, including 19,200 in Hitsats and Shimelba.

a256.speaker: Dr Sidi Ould Tah, president of the Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA)
a256.name: Dr Sidi Ould Tah
a256.title: president of the Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA)
a256.speech: Gave the inaugural conference on the theme "The future of the African banking sector: opportunities and challenges towards 2035", holding that the challenge is to reconcile technological innovation with the specific needs of African markets, while promoting financial inclusion.

a256.speaker: Dr Ngueto Tiraina Yambaye, Director General of FAGACE, elected head of the Club of Directors of Banks and Credit Institutions of Africa
a256.name: Dr Ngueto Tiraina Yambaye
a256.title: Director General of FAGACE, elected head of the Club of Directors of Banks and Credit Institutions of Africa
a256.speech: Reaffirmed FAGACE's commitment to supporting financial institutions in this transition towards a more innovative and resilient future, while urging sustained collaboration: "FAGACE will continue to play its role as an accelerator by mobilising the resources needed to finance structuring projects. But we cannot succeed alone. We need a strong partnership with you - bank directors, regulators, investors - to build a robust financial ecosystem, capable of supporting the sustainable development of the continent."

a257.speaker: Analysts interviewed by Brasil de Fato
a257.name: Analysts interviewed by Brasil de Fato
a257.speech: For the analysts interviewed by Brasil de Fato, the role played by USAID should fall into the hands of other tools, among them big tech such as Elon Musk's X.

a257.speaker: Nildo Ouriques, professor in the department of economics of international relations at UFSC
a257.name: Nildo Ouriques
a257.title: professor in the department of economics of international relations at UFSC
a257.speech: "The humanitarian premise is only part of the cynicism of the various governments of the United States, whether Republican or Democrat. USAID is an ideological arm of North American imperialism."

a257.speaker: Nildo Ouriques, professor in the department of economics of international relations at UFSC
a257.name: Nildo Ouriques
a257.title: professor in the department of economics of international relations at UFSC
a257.speech: States that USAID paved the way for state terrorism throughout Latin America, such as the 1968 university reform in Brazil under the military dictatorship.

a257.speaker: Marco Fernandes, of the Tricontinental Institute
a257.name: Marco Fernandes
a257.title: of the Tricontinental Institute
a257.speech: "To soften hearts and minds, they now have big tech, they no longer need the little programmes of the 1960s, a legacy of the Cold War" ; "The empire will find other instruments. Having the algorithm, Meta and Instagram do not need USAID."

a257.speaker: Elon Musk, owner of X and member of the Trump government
a257.name: Elon Musk
a257.title: owner of X and member of the Trump government
a257.speech: Said that this agency was "a nest of worms" and had to be closed.

a257.speaker: Marco Rubio, appointed by Trump to head USAID
a257.name: Marco Rubio
a257.title: appointed by Trump to head USAID
a257.speech: Said he would put an end to USAID's "insubordination" towards the far-right president: "In many cases, USAID takes part in programmes that go against what we are trying to do with our national strategy."

a257.speaker: Giorgio Romano, professor of international relations and economics at the Federal University of ABC (UFABC)
a257.name: Giorgio Romano
a257.title: professor of international relations and economics at the Federal University of ABC (UFABC)
a257.speech: Says that USAID's structure is "Democratic at its base", that is to say a rival of the Republicans of the current government ; "It is a political question. Trump does not want the powers of the state to be controlled by a Democratic bureaucracy. He must put things in order just as he must reduce the funding of the World Bank, which is also in the hands of the Democrats."

a257.speaker: Luis Eduardo da Rocha Fernandes, doctor (Ance)
a257.name: Luis Eduardo da Rocha Fernandes
a257.title: doctor (Ance)
a257.speech: States that the dismantling of USAID is a measure intended to mobilise the electoral base of the Republican who "clearly has a far-right project within an international coordination" ; "Several United States agencies and bodies are carrying out reforms to align themselves with this strategic concept of greater closeness with the far-right and neo-fascist groups of the whole world" ; "We should not delude ourselves and think that this is good news, because the budget for what is called 'humanitarian aid' can be reassigned to other far-right movements more aligned with Trump's conservative project, such as the fight against the right to abortion throughout the world, for example."

a326.speaker: Fitch (ratings agency)
a326.name: Fitch (ratings agency)
a326.speech: Acknowledges that the suspension of USAID support to Mozambique contributed to the worsening of the foreign-currency shortage in the country, given that the agency’s disbursements represented about 3% of Gross Domestic Product; in February it classified Mozambique as having a very high level of default risk relative to other issuers or obligations within the same country, and states that USAID’s exit will have aggravated the foreign-exchange crisis. “The shortage of foreign currency increased in 2025, partly due to the fall in external disbursements to the Government and the suspension of USAID”, writes Fitch, stating that the American agency disbursed 586 million dollars in support in 2024.

a326.speaker: Fitch (ratings agency)
a326.name: Fitch (ratings agency)
a326.speech: Points to the increase in mandatory conversion of export revenues into local currency, from 30% to 50%, which should help ease pressure on the foreign-currency shortage, and to the expectation of a new programme with the International Monetary Fund, which should relieve the pressure.

a326.speaker: Clésio Foia, economist
a326.name: Clésio Foia
a326.title: economist
a326.speech: Is not surprised by the assessment and says the country needs to redefine public policies to incubate an economy that is in deficit. “We are saying that the foreign exchange market is left with a deficit of 586 million dollars, which will put pressure on the interaction of market forces between the demand and supply of foreign currency, causing pressures as a consequence of the absence of this USAID funding” ; “First, we are talking about inflationary pressures, because if we have an absence of foreign currency it means there will be pressure on the exchange market, and the exchange rate will react progressively in favour of the foreign currency.”

a326.speaker: Clésio Foia, economist
a326.name: Clésio Foia
a326.title: economist
a326.speech: Said the weight of external debt is another ill afflicting the national economy and that the country must start worrying about the image it leaves for international investors. “First, it is giving a signal that there needs to be some improvement in what has to do with management, both of public affairs and governmental transparency, but it is also posing a challenge regarding the objectives of the Mozambican State, to start thinking about public indebtedness oriented towards public investment.”

a342.speaker: Atiku Abubakar, Former Vice-President of Nigeria
a342.name: Atiku Abubakar
a342.title: Former Vice-President of Nigeria
a342.speech: Asked the people of Rivers State to reject the Saturday local government election, describing it as an "absurdity and a travesty to the very notion of elective democracy" ; said in a statement posted on his social media pages, "The local government election conducted by the occupation government in Rivers State is an awful absurdity and a travesty to the very notion of elective democracy." ; "By the shameful and shambolic manner in which the occupation government went ahead to conduct local government elections in Rivers State, it is clear that the ruling APC is not leaving anyone in doubt that it is prepared to throw caution to the wind in order to achieve an inordinate political advantage."

a342.speaker: Atiku Abubakar, Former Vice-President of Nigeria
a342.name: Atiku Abubakar
a342.title: Former Vice-President of Nigeria
a342.speech: Called on well-meaning Nigerians, the international community and partners of Nigeria to rise up against the "dangerous curve that the President Bola Tinubu regime is taking our dear country"; said it had become necessary to call the attention of well-meaning Nigerians and the international community to that curve.

a342.speaker: Atiku Abubakar, Former Vice-President of Nigeria
a342.name: Atiku Abubakar
a342.title: Former Vice-President of Nigeria
a342.speech: Called on all opposition parties in Rivers State to reject the local government election on the "premise that the occupation government that conducted the exercise is extraneous to our laws, with absolutely no legitimacy to undertake such a crucial and sensitive assignment." ; "In the same breath, I wish to share my unflinching solidarity with the good people of Rivers State, who are currently victims of political brigandry to a power cabal which is bent on overturning their democratic rights at all cost."

a395.speaker: Tiawon Saye Gongloe, Liberian human rights advocate, politician, assistant professor of law at the University of Liberia and 2023 presidential candidate
a395.name: Tiawon Saye Gongloe
a395.title: Liberian human rights advocate, politician, assistant professor of law at the University of Liberia and 2023 presidential candidate
a395.speech: Exalted the extraordinary legacy of Liberia's first president, Joseph Jenkins Roberts, whose diplomacy, resilience and faith he said "secured Liberia's place on the global stage" ; "Today, we gather in unity and pride to celebrate the birthday of a remarkable man who shaped the destiny of our beloved nation: Joseph Jenkins Roberts, our first President and, for many, Liberia's greatest leader. His life's story is not merely a chapter in our history-it is a resounding testament to the power of vision, diplomacy, leadership, and unwavering devotion to our nation's progress." ; "At a moment when the eyes of the world were upon us, Joseph Jenkins Roberts dared to do the impossible. He boldly traveled to Europe, meeting with Queen Victoria, Napoleon III, and other European heads of state. In these historic encounters, he pressed for recognition of our sovereignty." ; Recalled that under the banner of the American Colonization Society, Roberts first served as governor, then on July 26, 1847 became the first President of the Republic of Liberia, and that Roberts later became the first President of Liberia College, which would evolve into the University of Liberia, bequeathing his entire estate for the education of the children of the land ; Said Roberts' greatest legacy was perhaps not only in the recognition he brought to Liberia but in the generosity of his spirit and the enduring example he set for leadership ; Said Roberts' bold steps in securing independence saved Liberia from the fate of many African nations carved apart during the Berlin Conference of 1884, and his humility after high office-choosing to become a teacher-speaks to a man who believed profoundly in the transformative power of education.

a395.speaker: Tiawon Saye Gongloe, Liberian human rights advocate and politician
a395.name: Tiawon Saye Gongloe
a395.title: Liberian human rights advocate and politician
a395.speech: "Moreover, he led a corruption-free government-one that served the people rather than exploited them-demonstrating that true leadership is rooted in integrity and the conviction that government exists to uplift citizens, not to enrich a select few. Imagine if every Liberian leader who followed had given even a portion of their own fortunes in support of our youth! The need for foreign aid in education might have been drastically reduced-perhaps eliminated altogether."

a395.speaker: Tiawon Saye Gongloe, Liberian human rights advocate and politician
a395.name: Tiawon Saye Gongloe
a395.title: Liberian human rights advocate and politician
a395.speech: Called on Liberians to emulate Roberts: "His acts of benevolence and foresight still reverberate across Liberia, channeling hope and promise into the hearts of young minds," adding: "So let us not only honor Joseph Jenkins Roberts with wreaths and tributes; let us learn from his leadership." ; Noted that in these times, when challenges loom large-from economic hurdles to educational shortcomings, "we can draw inspiration from his decisive leadership, his profound diplomacy, his unyielding honesty, and his boundless compassion"; said Roberts' leadership and charity remind Liberians that service to fellow citizens is the true mark of greatness ; "In Roberts' legacy, we see a Liberian dream that must never wane-a belief in ourselves, in our capacity to shape our own destiny, and in the undeniable power of unity and shared sacrifice. On this day-March 15, 2025-I call upon every Liberian, from the highest echelons of government to the humblest corners of our communities, to channel the spirit of Joseph Jenkins Roberts." ; Said the legacy projects include investing in education and willing resources to uplift future generations, and promoting decisive and visionary leadership, saying "a leader's true worth is measured by the tangible empowerment of their people"; said Roberts will be remembered for encouraging diplomacy and unity because "Our founder's tireless efforts for international recognition highlight the power of dialogue, perseverance, and unity of purpose"; spoke of Roberts' upholding of integrity in governance, admonishing leaders to follow his example by putting citizens first, resisting corruption, and using power to foster development and peace; said the ex-president fostered generosity and compassion, be it in public office, business, or civil society and that "we each hold the power to transform lives by sharing our knowledge, our resources, and our love for Liberia" ; "As we commemorate Joseph Jenkins Roberts, may we remember him not merely as a towering historical figure but as a beacon shining a path forward for our nation. His example teaches us that progress is possible when guided by integrity and selfless devotion. By celebrating his birthday, we celebrate the timeless values of independence, education, and service that he personified so well." ; Called on Liberians to observe March 15 as more than a ceremony but a time to rekindle "our determination to uphold and protect the promise he envisioned: a Liberia united by purpose, enriched by knowledge, and revered among nations for our dedication to one another" ; "On this day, I want all Liberians to accept the fact that government is a place to serve, not to steal! It is only with the acceptance of this fact by the Liberian people will a better Liberia be possible. Long Live the Spirit of Joseph Jenkins Roberts! Long LIVE!"

a724.speaker: Office of the Governor of Central Equatoria (statement)
a724.name: Office of the Governor of Central Equatoria (statement)
a724.speech: According to a statement from his office, the governor’s tour is aimed at consolidating durable peace, unity, and security in Central Equatoria.

a724.speaker: Francis Luwala, Secretary General of the Central Equatoria state government
a724.name: Francis Luwala
a724.title: Secretary General of the Central Equatoria state government
a724.speech: “The Governor is travelling in this significant trip by road because he wants to acquaint himself with the security situation across the State, understand the life of our people and the State road infrastructure” ; “This journey is also to give hope to our people on how much the government is concerned about the situation on ground among several reasons.”

a724.speaker: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)
a724.name: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)
a724.speech: Said it strongly condemns the attack against health workers in an area where people already face difficulty accessing healthcare, after suspending all its outreach activities in Yei in September following what it termed as a critical security incident involving its staff and staff from a partner organization.

a724.speaker: Augustino Jadalla, Governor of Central Equatoria
a724.name: Augustino Jadalla
a724.title: Governor of Central Equatoria
a724.speech: Following his appointment in May 2024, said he would relocate his office from county to county on a monthly basis to “acquaint” himself with the people and “implement the SPLM vision of taking towns to the people.”

a724.speaker: Augustino Jadalla, Governor of Central Equatoria
a724.name: Augustino Jadalla
a724.title: Governor of Central Equatoria
a724.speech: During a parliamentary session in September 2024, addressed the recurrent reports of Ugandan encroachment into South Sudan’s Kajo-keji County, attributing it to displacement of natives to refugee camps and “vulnerability of the bordering communities” resulting from lack of services; according to him, the displacement of the natives to neighbouring Uganda coupled with lack of services has led to the border exploitation of the community; said encouraging the return of refugees to Kajo-Keji County, and delivery of services to the community are two of his most important plans to minimize the border encroachment.

a787.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, former President of Ghana and 2024 NDC flagbearer (Facebook post)
a787.name: John Dramani Mahama
a787.title: former President of Ghana and 2024 NDC flagbearer (Facebook post)
a787.speech: Expressed deep disappointment and worry at the loss of $190 million meant for private sector participation in Ghana's electricity distribution under the US Millennium Compact, saying the "corrupt, 'yenkyendi', and cronyistic governance practices" spearheaded by President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo and Vice President Dr. Mahamudu Bawumia led to the loss: "It's disheartening to learn that the $190 million we negotiated for private sector participation in electricity distribution under the US Millennium Compact has been lost due to Nana Addo and Bawumia's corrupt, 'yenkyendi', and cronyistic governance practices. This is unacceptable, and we deserve better as a people."

a787.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, former President of Ghana and 2024 NDC flagbearer (Facebook post)
a787.name: John Dramani Mahama
a787.title: former President of Ghana and 2024 NDC flagbearer (Facebook post)
a787.speech: Pledged that he "will work diligently to enhance private sector efficiency in the electricity distribution system, including metering, revenue management, and fault response" when re-elected president, and promised to "ensure a thorough investigation of the PDS [Power Distribution Services] scandal to hold those involved accountable" ; "My administration will prioritise accountability... We can work together to build a brighter future for Ghana's power sector that benefits citizens and businesses. Let's stand together, fight against corruption and cronyism, and work towards building the Ghana we want."

a787.speaker: US government
a787.name: US government
a787.speech: Halted the transfer of the funds, stating that private sector participation was a central reform under MCC's Ghana Power Compact.

a1167.speaker: Anonymous (quoted saying)
a1167.name: Anonymous (quoted saying)
a1167.speech: "Great leaders do not give excuses for failure but find the reasons to succeed, against all odds."

a1167.speaker: Alex Otti, Governor of Abia State
a1167.name: Alex Otti
a1167.title: Governor of Abia State
a1167.speech: He promised to ensure that salaries and all entitlements are paid latest by the 28th of each month and has so far kept to his promise.

a1167.speaker: Alex Otti, Governor of Abia State
a1167.name: Alex Otti
a1167.title: Governor of Abia State
a1167.speech: Declared from his first day in office to revolutionalize the sector [infrastructure].

a1167.speaker: Alex Otti, Governor of Abia State
a1167.name: Alex Otti
a1167.title: Governor of Abia State
a1167.speech: While declaring open the renovated Abia state General Hospital, Amachara in September, 2023 the people's governor reiterated his government's commitment to making quality healthcare delivery affordable and accessible. He has pledged to sanitize the drug distribution system in the state while making sure that the welfare of all the medical staff in the state a matter of priority... As he rightly noted, the plans are on to strengthen the primary, secondary and tertiary arms of the health sector.

a1167.speaker: Alex Otti, Governor of Abia State
a1167.name: Alex Otti
a1167.title: Governor of Abia State
a1167.speech: Calling on other state governors to take a cue and light up Nigeria from the decades of demonic darkness.

a1182.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.name: Ndiviwe Mphothulo
a1182.title: President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.speech: Said he is not okay with the phenomenon of lambasting the country's pre-eminent struggle heroes. "You see it more and more, this thing of South Africans labelling Mandela a sell-out, calling Mamphela Ramphele a sell-out, and others. People need to start telling us about themselves first, like 'I am Thabo from Taung, I helped this many marginalised black people in my village and township, and that is why I hold this view'. Activism is hard, most have no idea."

a1182.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.name: Ndiviwe Mphothulo
a1182.title: President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.speech: On growing up in Jabavu, Soweto: "Some of the boys I knew would slip into nearby white suburbs like this one at night to do house-breaking. They called it hausa hausa, it was like a badge of pride." ; "Kung fu films at Eyethu cinema, in neighbouring Mofolo." ; "Swimming in the Jabavu pool, which everyone called Jakes." ; "Games of five-a-side in the yard of the Lutheran church on our street." ; "Big fights in the early hours: Mike Tyson, George Foreman and Roberto Duran." ; "Prayers that ended with 'Ha le lakatsa ho tseba' (If you want to know about the gospel), our neighbours' favourite hymn."

a1182.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.name: Ndiviwe Mphothulo
a1182.title: President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.speech: On his family and upbringing: "I was born into a culture of activism, just as my parents were born into it." ; "It was second nature, I think. Her parents founded the church and school in Qunu in the Eastern Cape, the very same school that Nelson Mandela attended." ; "My grandmother, Tandiwe Zidlele, was already bedridden by that time but she commanded so much respect, people from all over would come to her for help. She didn't have much but she would feed people, open the house to people. She instilled that spirit in us children." ; "She was such a brave woman. She would be arrested, dragged around, and the following week you find her picketing outside court. If young people were hurt she would get them to doctors, and get arrested again herself. She taught us to stand up for what is right, irrespective of the consequences."

a1182.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.name: Ndiviwe Mphothulo
a1182.title: President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.speech: On mediating a hijacking at 16: "It is hard to imagine then the power that students had then." ; "He said, 'We've got an issue at a school called Lebone [secondary], some of the students have hijacked the bakery truck.' So I went there and I met the guy who hijacked the truck, and I asked him why he did it and he said, 'We were hungry.' After some discussion, he agreed to return it." ; "It also made me realise, you know, if this is what it takes to get back a bakery truck in Mofolo, what must it have been like for Mandela and others, leading the entire revolution? That is why I always say, before you criticise those figures, first understand what it means to be an activist."

a1182.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.name: Ndiviwe Mphothulo
a1182.title: President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.speech: On schooling and choosing medicine: "It was the Eastern Cape influence, I think — for my family there, education was paramount." ; "Some said I should study law, due to my involvement in student politics. My English teacher said 'You can write, you must enrol in humanities at Fort Hare, become a professor.' But my maths, science and biology teachers said, 'No way is this one doing English'." ; "I saw that it was possible to cure tonsillitis and cut an appendix while also building communities. I realised that I would not be lost to activism if I chose to become a clinician, and so I enrolled for a bachelor of science at what was then the Medical University of Southern Africa (now Sefako Makgatho Health Sciences University), and got into medicine the following year."

a1182.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.name: Ndiviwe Mphothulo
a1182.title: President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.speech: On his quiet university years and internship: "I was so quiet, to the extent that people would say, 'What happened, bru, you were so involved, and now look at you.' I don't know, I think it was like a deep debriefing period for me, because from the age of 12 I had experienced a lot of things. I was telling someone that university was the first time I had not heard gunfire in a week. I could not explain it then, but I have since thought that perhaps I just wanted to be a child again, you know, because I hadn't really had that experience of normal living." ; "My registrar started to notice that I took an interest in patients' social issues, so in each block I did they would say, 'This one has got these social issues, Ndiviwe will deal with her. He's our social worker.' In the orthopaedic ward you would get patients who'd fallen off trains having traumatic amputations, and there would be stress about going to work — 'I've been here so long what will my employer say,' and that sort of thing — and I'd call the employer for a conversation."

a1182.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.name: Ndiviwe Mphothulo
a1182.title: President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.speech: On HIV and TB work at Taung Hospital: "I agreed, and within months found myself working in the hospital's TB ward, after it became clear that a high percentage of the patients we were working up for ARVs already had TB." ; "It was a crash course. I learned a lot, and I enjoyed the work." ; "The cure rates for MDR-TB at this time were bad, about 50-55%, and although the drugs we had to fight with were not perfect, I saw our patients struggling more with transport, a lack of food in the home, unemployment, stigma — social issues, in other words. I thought, 'No man, let me come with some initiatives, even if it requires me to fight with management a little bit.'" ; "It was unbelievable, people were so interested, asking: how can a rural hospital have such high treatment cure outcomes?"

a1182.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.name: Ndiviwe Mphothulo
a1182.title: President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.speech: On social barriers facing MDR-TB patients and the support programme he designed: "Something she said has stayed with me." ; "She used to say a combination of poverty and illiteracy is an impairment, so be patient, it's an impairment. A lot of MDR-TB patients are impaired in this way. They are sick, they are poor, they have illiteracy problems. It isn't enough to say, 'Go to your nearest Sassa office, apply for a disability grant'. No, for someone like this, Sassa is an almost impossible mountain to climb." ; "What this country needs is a support programme that basically says, we will hold your hand once you are diagnosed with TB. If you qualify for food parcels, we will get you food parcels. If you qualify for a disability grant, we will get you your disability grant. That is what I have tried to design."

a1182.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.name: Ndiviwe Mphothulo
a1182.title: President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.speech: On the US funding cuts and the government's response to the HIV crisis: "They [senior government figures] will say 'Let's go to the clinic, we will show you shelves stocked with ARVs'. In other words, there is no crisis. But this misses the point. Ending HIV as a public health issue, which is something we were on track to do by 2030, is not just about pills on shelves. It's about interventions targeting the most at risk populations, like young women, sex workers, men who have sex with men. It's about the continuation of South Africa's cutting edge research into HIV. These are the areas of the response that have been hit by the funding cuts, and without urgent action we risk reversing a lot of our gains in the fight against HIV." ; Communicated in writing to Deputy President Paul Mashatile, chairperson of the South African National Aids Council, the idea that government should strongly consider reprising its approach to the Covid-19 pandemic, appointing multi-sectoral advisory committees to work on the various facets of the crisis in HIV. ; "Our message is clear: We think they are too relaxed — their response to date has been inadequate."

a1182.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.name: Ndiviwe Mphothulo
a1182.title: President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.speech: Said that if he could be granted one wish it would be that the government heed the warning of medical activists: "If you look at the history of activism in the HIV space in the country, it started with lone voices in the mid-80s, who were written off as lunatics. In the early 90s more voices joined the chorus — even politicians like Chris Hani were saying there is a problem here — but the government kept its ears closed, and it was the same in the early 2000s, even in the face of so many deaths. Now we see history repeating itself. HIV activists have raised the alarm, saying there is a problem, and the government is once again in a state of denial."

a1182.speaker: Ndiviwe Mphothulo, President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.name: Ndiviwe Mphothulo
a1182.title: President of the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society
a1182.speech: On his book Medicine & Activism: "When I entered medicine it satisfied my science and maths teachers, and when I returned to activism I pleased those who were politically inclined. All that remained was my English teacher, so ja, now he can be pleased, too."

a1182.speaker: Simulation modelling analysis published in the Annals of Internal Medicine
a1182.name: Simulation modelling analysis published in the Annals of Internal Medicine
a1182.speech: Suggests cuts to the US President's Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) programme could cost South Africa 565 000 new HIV infections and 601 000 more deaths from the virus by 2034.

a1185.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO) data
a1185.name: World Health Organisation (WHO) data
a1185.speech: The most recent data reveals Africa accounted for about 95% of the 249 million malaria cases and 608 000 deaths worldwide in 2022, with children under five accounting for 80% of deaths in the region.

a1185.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a1185.name: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a1185.speech: Says Anopheles stephensi is key to an "unprecedented surge" in Ethiopia, from 4.1 million malaria cases and 527 deaths last year to 7.3 million cases and 1 157 deaths between 1 January and 20 October 2024.

a1185.speaker: Meera Venkatesan, malaria division chief for the United States Agency for International Development (USAID)
a1185.name: Meera Venkatesan
a1185.title: malaria division chief for the United States Agency for International Development (USAID)
a1185.speech: "The invasion and spread of Anopheles stephensi has the potential to change the malaria landscape in Africa, and reverse decades of progress we've made towards malaria control."

a1185.speaker: Meera Venkatesan, malaria division chief for USAID
a1185.name: Meera Venkatesan
a1185.title: malaria division chief for USAID
a1185.speech: "The increased transmission that stephensi is driving could potentially help accelerate the spread of other threats, such as drug resistance or another mutation in the parasite that leads it to be less detectable by our most widely-used diagnostics."

a1185.speaker: A 2020 study
a1185.name: A 2020 study
a1185.speech: Warns it could eventually reach 126 million city-dwellers across Africa.

a1185.speaker: Charles Mbogo, president of the Pan-African Mosquito Control Association
a1185.name: Charles Mbogo
a1185.title: president of the Pan-African Mosquito Control Association
a1185.speech: "We don't yet fully understand the biology and behaviour of this mosquito." ; "Possibly it is climate-driven, and requires high temperatures, but much more research is needed." ; He called for increased funding for capturing and testing mosquitos, and educating the public on prevention measures, such as covering water receptacles.

a1185.speaker: Charles Mbogo, president of the Pan-African Mosquito Control Association
a1185.name: Charles Mbogo
a1185.title: president of the Pan-African Mosquito Control Association
a1185.speech: Said "more political will" is needed on the lack of coordination between African governments. "We share information as scientists with colleagues in neighbouring countries." ; "But we need to reach the higher level. We need cross-border collaborations, data-sharing."

a1185.speaker: Dorothy Achu, WHO's head of tropical and vector-borne diseases in Africa
a1185.name: Dorothy Achu
a1185.title: WHO's head of tropical and vector-borne diseases in Africa
a1185.speech: "The arrival of resistance is imminent." ; Said WHO is working with countries to diversify treatment programmes to delay resistance.

a1185.speaker: Dorothy Achu, WHO's head of tropical and vector-borne diseases in Africa
a1185.name: Dorothy Achu
a1185.title: WHO's head of tropical and vector-borne diseases in Africa
a1185.speech: Said WHO is working on "a more continental approach" to the lack of coordination between African governments.

a1270.speaker: Residents in rural areas of Awdal and Salal
a1270.name: Residents in rural areas of Awdal and Salal
a1270.speech: report the widespread death of livestock and the migration of families in search of water and pasture.

a1270.speaker: Government officials (Somaliland)
a1270.name: Government officials (Somaliland)
a1270.speech: say the pattern reflects the increasing severity of climate shocks in the Horn of Africa, where rain-dependent economies are vulnerable to prolonged dry spells.

a1270.speaker: Humanitarian agencies and local aid workers
a1270.name: Humanitarian agencies and local aid workers
a1270.speech: warn that the crisis is being exacerbated by a sharp decline in foreign assistance.

a1270.speaker: USAID
a1270.name: USAID
a1270.speech: has pulled back operations in the region, citing global funding shortfalls.

a1270.speaker: Somaliland officials
a1270.name: Somaliland officials
a1270.speech: stress that a broader, coordinated effort—including international donors, local businesses, and the diaspora—is needed to prevent a full-scale humanitarian catastrophe.

a1270.speaker: Aid organizations
a1270.name: Aid organizations
a1270.speech: are urging both emergency aid and long-term solutions such as investment in sustainable water systems, climate-resilient agriculture, and early warning infrastructure to build resilience against future shocks.

a1270.speaker: Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro, President of Somaliland
a1270.name: Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro
a1270.title: President of Somaliland
a1270.speech: said the government would continue to monitor the situation closely and revise its response strategy as needed. For now, he warned, the focus must remain on saving lives. "Our people are suffering from hunger and thirst," he said. "We must come together, as a nation, to meet this challenge head-on."

a1285.speaker: Those who spoke to Weekend Trust (residents/stakeholders)
a1285.name: Those who spoke to Weekend Trust (residents/stakeholders)
a1285.speech: have called for accountability and renewed vigour from various stakeholders to address the problem.

a1285.speaker: Report, 'Water Sanitation and Hygiene National Outcome Routine Mapping'
a1285.name: Report
a1285.title: 'Water Sanitation and Hygiene National Outcome Routine Mapping'
a1285.speech: A recent report suggests that approximately 60 per cent of Nigerians, or roughly 110 million people, lack access to safe drinking water. According to the report titled, 'Water Sanitation and Hygiene National Outcome Routine Mapping', nearly a third of Nigerians don't have access to basic supply of water.

a1285.speaker: Federal Ministry of Water Resources and Sanitation
a1285.name: Federal Ministry of Water Resources and Sanitation
a1285.speech: says it is the sole responsibility of the state government to provide clean and safe water in their respective states.

a1285.speaker: Community members of Korokpa, Paikoro LGA, Niger State
a1285.name: Community members of Korokpa
a1285.title: Paikoro LGA, Niger State
a1285.speech: told Weekend Trust that Elizabeth is one of many victims who have lost their lives in search of water for their families.

a1285.speaker: Abigail Idoko, aunt of the late Elizabeth Peter
a1285.name: Abigail Idoko
a1285.title: aunt of the late Elizabeth Peter
a1285.speech: "They, Elizabeth and her siblings went to the river because there was no other place to get water. The borehole is faulty, and the water vendors couldn't pump water due to lack of electricity. This is what we face always."

a1285.speaker: Isah Mohammed, resident of Korokpa
a1285.name: Isah Mohammed
a1285.title: resident of Korokpa
a1285.speech: "Without power, commercial borehole operators can't pump water because of high cost of fuel. That's why children go to the river. We have very few wells, and even then, people beg just to get a bucket or two."

a1285.speaker: Rabi Danladi, resident
a1285.name: Rabi Danladi
a1285.title: resident
a1285.speech: "We fetch from the Chanchaga River, where animals also graze and drink from. This is the same water we drink, cook, and bath with. Sometimes, human waste floats by as we fetch water, but we have no choice but to fetch the water." ; She said every year people die in the river, calling for government's attention.

a1285.speaker: Malama Amina Sadiq, resident of Gbeganu area, Minna
a1285.name: Malama Amina Sadiq
a1285.title: resident of Gbeganu area, Minna
a1285.speech: shared how her children sometimes go to school without bathing. "Some days, we can't even find water vendors," she said.

a1285.speaker: Malam Salihu Ibrahim
a1285.name: Malam Salihu Ibrahim
a1285.speech: "The crisis is not limited to Minna. In rural communities such as Lemu, the headquarters of Gbako LGA, residents face similar challenges with women and children having to wake up before dawn to search for water."

a1285.speaker: Zainab Yunusa, Public Relations Officer of the Niger State Water and Sewage Corporation
a1285.name: Zainab Yunusa
a1285.title: Public Relations Officer of the Niger State Water and Sewage Corporation
a1285.speech: said the government was working to resolve the situation. She attributed part of the water shortages to ongoing road construction projects that have disrupted pipelines. Mrs Yunusa, however, added that communities not yet connected to the water board would need to make financial commitments to get linked to the network.

a1285.speaker: Residents of Ranzaga, Ungogo LGA, Kano State
a1285.name: Residents of Ranzaga
a1285.title: Ungogo LGA, Kano State
a1285.speech: said they have been without water for years which leaves them at the mercy of water vendors.

a1285.speaker: Alhaji Bela, resident of Ranzaga
a1285.name: Alhaji Bela
a1285.title: resident of Ranzaga
a1285.speech: "We have been without water for as long as I can remember. We just buy from vendors who also depend on boreholes."

a1285.speaker: Salisu Karfi, resident of Karfi town
a1285.name: Salisu Karfi
a1285.title: resident of Karfi town
a1285.speech: "Wells are our main source of water here in Karfi."

a1285.speaker: Kano State Ministry of Water Resources
a1285.name: Kano State Ministry of Water Resources
a1285.speech: had last month assured residents that the scarcity would soon be history, saying new pumping machines procured by the ministry had arrived the country and would be installed to improve water supply.

a1285.speaker: Abba Kabir Yusuf, Governor of Kano State
a1285.name: Abba Kabir Yusuf
a1285.title: Governor of Kano State
a1285.speech: had ordered immediate construction of boreholes in Danya and Kyallin Bulla villages of Bichi LGA.

a1285.speaker: Umar Haruna Doguwa, Kano State Commissioner for Water Resources
a1285.name: Umar Haruna Doguwa
a1285.title: Kano State Commissioner for Water Resources
a1285.speech: said proactive measures have been implored to revive the existing water reservoirs in the state to improve supply.

a1285.speaker: Residents of Agbor, Ika-South and Ika-North East LGAs, Delta State
a1285.name: Residents of Agbor
a1285.title: Ika-South and Ika-North East LGAs, Delta State
a1285.speech: say potable water is only for those who can afford to drill boreholes.

a1285.speaker: Ogaga Ovie, resident of Okuama, Delta State
a1285.name: Ogaga Ovie
a1285.title: resident of Okuama, Delta State
a1285.speech: "It's surprising that Delta State is rich in water resources, yet many of us lack access to clean drinking water. We buy water every day just to survive," he said.

a1285.speaker: Toritseju Wayimi, resident of Warri
a1285.name: Toritseju Wayimi
a1285.title: resident of Warri
a1285.speech: "In these areas, people travel to the cities to buy sachet and bottled water, as well as jerry cans of water because their only natural source is salt water."

a1285.speaker: Doose Nyinongo, resident of Kighir, Makurdi LGA, Benue State
a1285.name: Doose Nyinongo
a1285.title: resident of Kighir, Makurdi LGA, Benue State
a1285.speech: "We go to a neighbouring community, where a private well never runs dry. The queue is always long because everyone in Kighir depends on it. The well owner fetches for her household first before allowing others to collect water, free of charge," she explained. ; Nyinongo added that her younger siblings' education is being affected, as they sometimes miss school entirely or arrive late, depending on when they return from fetching water.

a1285.speaker: Katie Denen, resident of a suburb of Gboko LGA
a1285.name: Katie Denen
a1285.title: resident of a suburb of Gboko LGA
a1285.speech: "We trek long distances in search of water, often digging into stream beds. Many times, we stay up all night just to collect water from available spots. It's a truly terrible situation."

a1285.speaker: Adeyi, resident of Otukpo
a1285.name: Adeyi
a1285.title: resident of Otukpo
a1285.speech: "Morning and night, we trek long distances to fetch water that is not only smelly but also muddy. It is barely suitable for washing, let alone drinking. But that's what we drink. Most times, members of my household fall sick with typhoid, diarrhoea, and cholera, and I'm told it's because of the contaminated water." ; "But what can we do? We rely on this muddy water sourced from streams for washing, bathing, and cooking. Whenever it's the dry season like this time around, we have to go even farther into digging the stream beds to fetch water, and we dig into the dry wells to find drinking water."

a1285.speaker: Ankeli Amanyi, resident of Otukpo
a1285.name: Ankeli Amanyi
a1285.title: resident of Otukpo
a1285.speech: said that if government can walk its talk by resuscitating the water works in the town, a lot would have been done to also save many from health and environmental hazards.

a1285.speaker: Odoh Ugwu, Benue State Commissioner for Water Resources, Environment and Climate Change
a1285.name: Odoh Ugwu
a1285.title: Benue State Commissioner for Water Resources, Environment and Climate Change
a1285.speech: said the government was committed to addressing water scarcity.

a1285.speaker: Lagos residents
a1285.name: Lagos residents
a1285.speech: have decried the shortage of water in their communities, saying they spend between N800 and N1,000 for 10 kegs of 25 litres of water.

a1285.speaker: Daniella Tokolo, Lagos resident
a1285.name: Daniella Tokolo
a1285.title: Lagos resident
a1285.speech: lamented that the lack of potable water has become a nightmare for most Lagosians, saying she buys 20 gallons for N2,000 and manages it for two weeks. "The way it works is that the price varies based on where you reside and the availability of power supply. So, because my apartment is upstairs, the vendor charges N800 for 10 gallons of 25kg, but N1,000 when there is no light," she said.

a1285.speaker: Modupe Philips, nursing mother, Lagos
a1285.name: Modupe Philips
a1285.title: nursing mother, Lagos
a1285.speech: narrated her struggles getting water, saying that she usually treks a few miles down her street to fetch water for daily consumption. "It is very hard to get water because from where I live, I trek to fetch water. There's been no light for three to four days. We don't know the issues and it is not easy waking up in the morning to fetch water to bathe my baby," she said.

a1285.speaker: Residents of Nuku community, Abaji Area Council, FCT
a1285.name: Residents of Nuku community
a1285.title: Abaji Area Council, FCT
a1285.speech: say they spend the night at streams in order to get water which drips from under a rock as the only source of water for use in their homes.

a1285.speaker: Laraba Dangana, resident of Nuku community
a1285.name: Laraba Dangana
a1285.title: resident of Nuku community
a1285.speech: told our reporter that women usually leave their homes between 7pm and 8pm, after preparing the day's dinner to go to the stream which is almost dried up. "We often come here with our basins around that time; spread our wrappers to sleep on till the following morning just to get water from under the rock," she lamented. ; According to her, residents of the community face water scarcity, especially during the dry season yearly, adding that the struggle to get water in the community has continued to pose serious health and environmental risks to residents of the village.

a1285.speaker: Mairo Gwatana, housewife
a1285.name: Mairo Gwatana
a1285.title: housewife
a1285.speech: bemoaned the water problem facing the community, saying the development was a huge source of concern.

a1285.speaker: Yakubu Gideon, resident of Riwaza, Kwali Area Council
a1285.name: Yakubu Gideon
a1285.title: resident of Riwaza, Kwali Area Council
a1285.speech: said the incident happened when some herders moved their cows to contaminate a water pond serving the community.

a1285.speaker: Isah Zozo Kure, village head of Riwaza community
a1285.name: Isah Zozo Kure
a1285.title: village head of Riwaza community
a1285.speech: noted that lack of drinking water had been the major problem facing his people over the years. He confirmed that women always left their homes late in the evening in search of water and returned in the morning, a situation which has been a source of concern to their husbands. The village chief appealed to the FCT minister, Nyesom Wike, to intervene in the issue.

a1285.speaker: Official from the works department of the Kwali Area Council (anonymous)
a1285.name: Official from the works department of the Kwali Area Council (anonymous)
a1285.speech: confided in our reporter that the department had received reports on the challenges being faced by the communities in the area and had captured at least 10 communities in this year's budget. He said work would soon start in most of the communities.

a1285.speaker: Official attached to the Works Department in Bwari Area Council
a1285.name: Official attached to the Works Department in Bwari Area Council
a1285.speech: said work had commenced on boreholes in two communities within the council, adding that at least four other communities were captured by the council authorities this year.

a1285.speaker: Daniel Salka Audu, Acting General Manager of the FCT Water Board, and Lere Olayinka, Senior Special Assistant to the FCT Minister on communication and social media (non-response)
a1285.name: Daniel Salka Audu
a1285.title: Acting General Manager of the FCT Water Board, and Lere Olayinka, Senior Special Assistant to the FCT Minister on communication and social media (non-response)
a1285.speech: Several calls and text messages sent to both were neither answered nor responded to.

a1285.speaker: Daniel Salka Audu, Acting General Manager of the FCT Water Board
a1285.name: Daniel Salka Audu
a1285.title: Acting General Manager of the FCT Water Board
a1285.speech: he promised to send a team there to address the problem (when contacted a few weeks ago on the water situation in Maitama).

a1285.speaker: Source at the FCT Water Board headquarters in Area 3 (anonymous)
a1285.name: Source at the FCT Water Board headquarters in Area 3 (anonymous)
a1285.speech: said the situation would only improve when the Greater Abuja Water Project, aimed at connecting water from the board to more districts is completed.

a1285.speaker: Yahaya Ibrahim, resident of Maitama
a1285.name: Yahaya Ibrahim
a1285.title: resident of Maitama
a1285.speech: described the inconsistent public water supply as disastrous. He attributed the problem to broken water pipes and poor supply from the Usman Dam source. "We have resorted to buying water, which is costly and a health hazard. I reported to the FCT Water Board headquarters at Area 3 last week," he said. ; He added that most homes in the area relied on self-serving boreholes. "For those of us who don't have boreholes, we have to buy water regularly. The FCT minister should do the needful," he said.

a1285.speaker: Officials of the FCT Water Board
a1285.name: Officials of the FCT Water Board
a1285.speech: attributed the challenge to the topography of the district, saying the problem required heavy investment in the system upgrade.

a1285.speaker: Suleiman Ajayi, resident of Gwarinpa
a1285.name: Suleiman Ajayi
a1285.title: resident of Gwarinpa
a1285.speech: described the situation as worrisome, saying most people in his area now rely on water vendors, popularly known as mairuwa, to survive.

a1285.speaker: Coalition of water justice organisations and the Amalgamated Union of Public Corporations, Civil Service Technical and Recreational Services Employees (AUPCTRE)
a1285.name: Coalition of water justice organisations and the Amalgamated Union of Public Corporations
a1285.title: Civil Service Technical and Recreational Services Employees (AUPCTRE)
a1285.speech: have called on the federal government to declare a state of emergency in the water sector.

a1285.speaker: Report, 'Dry Taps: A Damning Verdict on the State of Water Facilities in Nigeria'
a1285.name: Report
a1285.title: 'Dry Taps: A Damning Verdict on the State of Water Facilities in Nigeria'
a1285.speech: The document assessed the state of water utilities in six states across Nigeria's geopolitical zones: Lagos, Oyo, Enugu, Edo, Kano, and Kogi.

a1285.speaker: Philip Jakpor, Executive Director of the Renevyln Development Initiative (RDI)
a1285.name: Philip Jakpor
a1285.title: Executive Director of the Renevyln Development Initiative (RDI)
a1285.speech: stated that they found that most major waterworks in the six states were providing inconsistent services and operating below their installed capacity. He noted that many of the mini and micro-waterworks in these states had either completely shut down, were neglected, or extensively vandalised, requiring a comprehensive overhaul of the sector.

a1285.speaker: Water vendors
a1285.name: Water vendors
a1285.speech: say they cover long distances under the scorching sun to get water for their customers. They said they charge customers based on the distance they have to cover to get water.

a1376.speaker: Jimmy Suah Shilue (opinion author)
a1376.name: Jimmy Suah Shilue (opinion author)
a1376.speech: Argues that with donor funding shrinking and development and humanitarian work fighting for survival, Liberia's NGOs must urgently rethink their dependence on grants, taking lessons from traditional churches that began with simple evangelical missions yet now own some of the nation's most prestigious schools, universities, hospitals, real estate, radio stations and thriving businesses. "With USAID suspending aid and global donors moving from 'aid' to 'trade,' the days of relying solely on grants are numbered." He warns that a country ranking 177 out of 193 on the HDI shows how fragile Liberia's recovery is, and that if NGOs do not adapt, many will simply disappear when the next funding crisis hits.

a1376.speaker: Jimmy Suah Shilue (opinion author)
a1376.name: Jimmy Suah Shilue (opinion author)
a1376.speech: Urges NGOs to engage in realistic and transparent discussion with funding partners to modify existing agreements, to build social enterprises, to collaborate with private sector actors and government ministries, to build alliances with diaspora investment groups for capital and technical support, and to align their mission statements with new revenue-generating ventures (eco-tourism lodges, waste recycling, consultancy, legal aid, vocational skills). He cites BRAC (Bangladesh), which funds 75% of its programs through social enterprises, Shining Hope for Communities (Kenya) and Sarvodaya (Sri Lanka) as global examples.

a1376.speaker: Jimmy Suah Shilue (opinion author)
a1376.name: Jimmy Suah Shilue (opinion author)
a1376.speech: Stresses that 'local ownership' is critical and must be prioritised, saying true sustainability requires local ownership and that NGOs must intentionally involve local actors in leadership, decision-making and accountability; he also laments that too often NGOs undermine each other in competition for scarce donor resources, which weakens the sector and erodes public trust. "The message is simple- learn from the churches. Move from aid to trade. In a volatile world, sustainability is the new salvation." ; "The choice is stark: adapt or fade."

a1413.speaker: Presidential proclamation signed by Donald Trump, US President
a1413.name: Presidential proclamation signed by Donald Trump
a1413.title: US President
a1413.speech: The new proclamation, which Trump signed last week, applies to citizens of Afghanistan, Myanmar, Chad, the Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Haiti, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan and Yemen. It also imposes heightened restrictions on people from Burundi, Cuba, Laos, Sierra Leone, Togo, Turkmenistan and Venezuela who are outside the US and don't hold a valid visa.

a1413.speaker: Guidance issued Friday to all US diplomatic missions
a1413.name: Guidance issued Friday to all US diplomatic missions
a1413.speech: The ban does not revoke visas previously issued to people from countries on the list, according to guidance issued Friday to all US diplomatic missions.

a1440.speaker: Gates Foundation
a1440.name: Gates Foundation
a1440.speech: has announced a new partnership with Indian manufacturer Hetero Labs to drive down the cost and expand access to a groundbreaking HIV prevention drug and accelerate access for millions of people in low- and middle-income countries; noted that only 18 per cent of those who could benefit from PrEP currently have access; further noted that it has already invested more than $80 million to speed up market readiness and shorten the timeline for generic entry of lenacapavir; noted that large-scale supply is expected as early as 2027, pending regulatory approvals.

a1440.speaker: Vamsi Krishna, managing director of the Hetero Group of Companies
a1440.name: Vamsi Krishna
a1440.title: managing director of the Hetero Group of Companies
a1440.speech: "Hetero is pleased to partner with the Gates Foundation to create a pathway for the sustainable and affordable supply of lenacapavir." ; "This collaboration reflects our commitment to ensuring access to innovative HIV medicines for patients in India and other low- and middle-income countries."

a1440.speaker: UNAIDS
a1440.name: UNAIDS
a1440.speech: According to UNAIDS, more than 40 million people are living with HIV worldwide. Despite progress since 2000, an estimated 1.3 million people contracted HIV in 2024, while over 600,000 died from AIDS-related illnesses.

a1440.speaker: Gates Foundation (statement)
a1440.name: Gates Foundation (statement)
a1440.speech: According to a statement from the foundation, lenacapavir was approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration in June and by the European Commission in August; it noted that the injection provides six months of protection in a single dose, offering a practical option for people unable to use daily oral PrEP because of stigma, adherence difficulties, or unreliable access to medicines.

a1440.speaker: Public health experts
a1440.name: Public health experts
a1440.speech: describe the drug as a transformative addition to the HIV prevention toolkit.

a1440.speaker: Modelling study published in The Lancet
a1440.name: Modelling study published in The Lancet
a1440.speech: found that scaling up lenacapavir to just four per cent of the population in high-burden countries could prevent up to 20 per cent of new infections.

a1440.speaker: Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative, and Wits RHI
a1440.name: Unitaid
a1440.title: the Clinton Health Access Initiative, and Wits RHI
a1440.speech: announced commitments with another Indian manufacturer, Dr Reddy's Laboratories, to further expand generic production.

a1440.speaker: Kate Hampton, CEO of the Children's Investment Fund Foundation
a1440.name: Kate Hampton
a1440.title: CEO of the Children's Investment Fund Foundation
a1440.speech: "The deals announced today on generics are a major step forward in ending the HIV epidemic."

a1440.speaker: Trevor Mundel, president of global health at the Gates Foundation
a1440.name: Trevor Mundel
a1440.title: president of global health at the Gates Foundation
a1440.speech: said affordability and equitable access are central to the partnership ; "Scientific advances like lenacapavir can help us end the HIV epidemic - if they are made accessible to people who can benefit from them the most." ; "We are committed to ensuring that those at highest risk, who can least afford it, aren't left behind."

a1440.speaker: Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria
a1440.name: Global Fund to Fight AIDS
a1440.title: Tuberculosis and Malaria
a1440.speech: has credited its work with helping reduce HIV infection rates by 82 per cent in supported countries since 2000.

a1440.speaker: Bill Gates, Chair of the Gates Foundation
a1440.name: Bill Gates
a1440.title: Chair of the Gates Foundation
a1440.speech: announced earlier this year that he would give away most of his wealth to accelerate progress in global health; said the foundation would spend $200 billion over the next two decades on ending preventable deaths of mothers and babies, tackling infectious diseases, and lifting millions out of poverty, before winding down its operations.

a1540.speaker: Professor Terry Taylor, American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.name: Professor Terry Taylor
a1540.title: American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.speech: "Malawi's role in the testing and rollout of the world's first malaria vaccine is well documented" ; "We helped prove its effectiveness in real-life conditions and now it's rolling out worldwide."

a1540.speaker: Professor Terry Taylor, American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.name: Professor Terry Taylor
a1540.title: American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.speech: Recalls how her work in Malawi began: "MSU requested me to develop a research project in a suitable country and Malawi was the perfect place" ; "I was drawn by the burden of severe malaria in children."

a1540.speaker: Professor Terry Taylor, American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.name: Professor Terry Taylor
a1540.title: American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.speech: On the retinal research conducted with ophthalmologist Dr Susan Lewallen: "It helped us distinguish between children truly suffering from cerebral malaria and those with other conditions like meningitis."

a1540.speaker: Professor Terry Taylor, American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.name: Professor Terry Taylor
a1540.title: American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.speech: On bringing Malawi's first MRI machine in 2008: "It was the only one in the country then" ; "It helped us understand the role of brain swelling in deaths caused by malaria."

a1540.speaker: Professor Terry Taylor, American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.name: Professor Terry Taylor
a1540.title: American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.speech: Says Malawi was far-sighted in making artemether-lumefantrine [LA] widely available in communities: "With rapid diagnostic tests, it meant a child in a village could get tested and treated immediately. Hospital admissions fell from over 400 to about 70 a year."

a1540.speaker: Professor Terry Taylor, American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.name: Professor Terry Taylor
a1540.title: American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.speech: Says "Malawi is home" and finds Malawians "friendly, welcoming, encouraging and remarkably cheerful" despite everyday challenges ; "I'm a permanent resident now; I've always felt at home here. I've watched trees we planted in 1986 grow tall. I've seen young researchers I mentored rise to lead their own labs. And I've seen how powerful it is when science and community work hand in hand."

a1540.speaker: Professor Terry Taylor, American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.name: Professor Terry Taylor
a1540.title: American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.speech: On her favourite Chichewa proverb, Mutu umodzi susenza denga (two heads are better than one): "It beautifully represents the collaborative spirit of all we've done here."

a1540.speaker: Professor Terry Taylor, American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.name: Professor Terry Taylor
a1540.title: American medical researcher and director of the Blantyre Malaria Project at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Kuhes)
a1540.speech: Advocates for Malawian-led research funding mechanisms: "There's so much talent here, I want to help create local support systems that allow these scientists to thrive independently."

a1540.speaker: Ministry of Health of Malawi
a1540.name: Ministry of Health of Malawi
a1540.speech: Asked her a simple question: "What is your top research priority?"

a1540.speaker: Professor Richard Mkandawire, National Planning Commission board chairperson
a1540.name: Professor Richard Mkandawire
a1540.title: National Planning Commission board chairperson
a1540.speech: Observes on Taylor's contribution: "This is an amazing story in combating the dreaded malaria disease. Her impact on the health systems is phenomenal and speaks to the Malawi 2063."

a1540.speaker: Dr Isabella Tirtowalujo, Michigan State University International Studies and Programme's Assistant Dean for Administration and Global Inclusion
a1540.name: Dr Isabella Tirtowalujo
a1540.title: Michigan State University International Studies and Programme's Assistant Dean for Administration and Global Inclusion
a1540.speech: "Michigan State University is proud to call Dr Taylor one of its esteemed faculty members as she embodies the very best qualities of what educators and health professionals ought to be."

a1572.speaker: Dr. Edward Lama Wonkeryor, Executive Director of the National Commission on Higher Education (NCHE), Liberia
a1572.name: Dr. Edward Lama Wonkeryor
a1572.title: Executive Director of the National Commission on Higher Education (NCHE), Liberia
a1572.speech: Affirmed the commitment of the Commission to excellence in the higher education sector of Liberia: "The National Commission on Higher Education remains committed to supporting this journey of excellence. We recognize the significance of this workshop in shaping not only the academic environment, but the lives of students who will benefit from your dedication." ; "As we conclude this transformative faculty and leadership development workshop, I am filled with both pride and optimism for the future of higher education in Liberia."

a1572.speaker: Dr. Edward Lama Wonkeryor, Executive Director of the National Commission on Higher Education (NCHE), Liberia
a1572.name: Dr. Edward Lama Wonkeryor
a1572.title: Executive Director of the National Commission on Higher Education (NCHE), Liberia
a1572.speech: Urged participants to keep applying what they had learned: "However, the trek does not end here. I encourage each of you to continue applying the skills and insights you have gained and to foster the collaborative spirit we have seen throughout this week. By sharing your experiences, challenges, and successes with one another, we create a strong network of leaders who are not only educators, but lifelong learners and change makers." ; "As we look to the future, remember that your roles as educators and administrators are essential. For example, you shape minds, build futures, and contribute to the very fabric of our society. I urge you all to take what you have learned, share it with your colleagues, and carry forward the momentum we have built together."

a1572.speaker: Dr. Edward Lama Wonkeryor, Executive Director of the National Commission on Higher Education (NCHE), Liberia
a1572.name: Dr. Edward Lama Wonkeryor
a1572.title: Executive Director of the National Commission on Higher Education (NCHE), Liberia
a1572.speech: Thanked the United States and USAID for their support: "Again, we cannot stop thanking the government and people of the United States of America, and USAID for the phenomenal supports provided to the Ministry of Education (MOE) and the National Commission on Higher Education (NCHE), to improve the quality of teachers' instructional delivery in our early childhood and primary schools. Thank you once again for your dedication to this noble cause. Let us continue working hand-in-hand to elevate higher education in Liberia." ; "On behalf of the National Commission on Higher Education, I would like to extend my heartfelt gratitude to USAID/TESTs for their support and to the dedicated facilitators from Mississippi State University (MSU) who have worked tirelessly over the past few days. Thank you to each participant who brought their commitment, curiosity, and energy into this program – your active engagement is what made this workshop a true success."

a1572.speaker: Dr. Edward Lama Wonkeryor, Executive Director of the National Commission on Higher Education (NCHE), Liberia
a1572.name: Dr. Edward Lama Wonkeryor
a1572.title: Executive Director of the National Commission on Higher Education (NCHE), Liberia
a1572.speech: Recounted that during the training important milestones were achieved: "From innovative teaching methodologies to critical leadership principles, we have covered a range of tools and strategies that will undoubtedly serve as catalysts for growth and improvement in our educational institutions." ; "I have heard from several of you about the insights you've gained and the plans you're eager to implement. This workshop has set the foundation for a brighter, more resilient education system—one that can rise to meet both national and global expectations."

a2076.speaker: Dr Gualbert Tolome, focal point of the LMG project at the Regional Institute of Public Health (IRSP)
a2076.name: Dr Gualbert Tolome
a2076.title: focal point of the LMG project at the Regional Institute of Public Health (IRSP)
a2076.speech: Gave extensive explanations about the project, saying it is a project initiated by USAID in collaboration with the Ministry of Health to improve performance within the health system, and that the system does not lack know-how ; "For a long time we always believed that the development of the health system would be due to financing. But the indicators do not change. It follows that the problem lies with the people who implement the strategies," concluding that this is what underlies the initiative of this project.

a2076.speaker: Dr Noel Moussiliou Paraiso, principal researcher on the project
a2076.name: Dr Noel Moussiliou Paraiso
a2076.title: principal researcher on the project
a2076.speech: "Despite the fact that the system does not lack know-how, it is emotional management, in order to achieve a result, that is lacking." He added that for the project the IRSP will train a pool of trainers who are senior officials of the Ministry of Health, whose mission will be to train in cascade at the operational level so that an interesting result can be achieved ; "To this are added notions on how to train adults."

a2076.speaker: Professor Michel Makoutode, director of the IRSP
a2076.name: Professor Michel Makoutode
a2076.title: director of the IRSP
a2076.speech: Welcomed the initiative and gave assurances that his institute will spare no effort to meet the expectations of the project's initiators: "The project is designed to support the Ministry of Health in its determination to improve the health system."

a2076.speaker: Justin Sossou, deputy secretary general of the Ministry of Health and representative of the Minister of Health
a2076.name: Justin Sossou
a2076.title: deputy secretary general of the Ministry of Health and representative of the Minister of Health
a2076.speech: Insisted on the need to achieve better performance through the shaping of people: "Health is vital for people. How do we come to an understanding in order to better meet demand; being always able to satisfy demand must be the credo. It is not a question of money or resources, but of shaping people to act for a good result, that is what counts. And in this respect every link in the chain must properly play its role, hence the need to question ourselves." He calls for a new dynamism that will make it possible to question many things that used to be done ; "The trainer has the heavy responsibility of being the torchbearer capable of convincing people about how to revise management."

a2102.speaker: National Health Laboratory Service (previously unpublished government data)
a2102.name: National Health Laboratory Service (previously unpublished government data)
a2102.speech: Showed that viral load testing fell by up to 21% among key groups in the last two months; the number of viral load tests conducted for people aged 15-24 fell by 17.2% in April compared to April last year, after dropping 7.8% year-on-year in March; total population testing was down 11.4% in April; maternal viral load testing was down 21.3% in April after falling 9.1% in March; early infant diagnostic testing was down 19.9% in April after falling 12.4% in March; and the percentage of people virally suppressed among those tested fell nationwide by 3.4% in March and 0.2% in April.

a2102.speaker: Four HIV experts
a2102.name: Four HIV experts
a2102.speech: Said the fall in viral load testing appeared to be due to the loss of U.S. funding.

a2102.speaker: Francois Venter, executive director of the Ezintsha Research Centre in Johannesburg
a2102.name: Francois Venter
a2102.title: executive director of the Ezintsha Research Centre in Johannesburg
a2102.speech: "This is pure, pure programmatic failure. And everyone should be alarmed when they see something like a 10 - 15% drop in the number of viral loads done just year on year and only in the space of three months in an incredibly stable program."

a2102.speaker: Foster Mohale, spokesperson for South Africa's Department of Health
a2102.name: Foster Mohale
a2102.title: spokesperson for South Africa's Department of Health
a2102.speech: Given a summary of the data, said more analysis was needed and that South Africa already had challenges with patient retention and viral load testing before the aid cuts.

a2102.speaker: HIV experts
a2102.name: HIV experts
a2102.speech: Have said for months that the health ministry was downplaying the impact of the funding loss in South Africa, and that a drop in testing figures might be an early warning sign - followed by a rise in new cases and deaths.

a2102.speaker: U.S. State Department
a2102.name: U.S. State Department
a2102.speech: Did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

a2102.speaker: Dvora Joseph Davey, epidemiologist working on maternal and infant HIV at the University of Cape Town
a2102.name: Dvora Joseph Davey
a2102.title: epidemiologist working on maternal and infant HIV at the University of Cape Town
a2102.speech: "The only thing that's really changed in this time period is the withdrawal of the PEPFAR funding support, which impacted directly on almost 10,000 health care providers, including doctors, nurses, community health workers, and HIV counselors that were key in the communities with the highest HIV prevalence and incidence in South Africa." ; Said the impact was clear at five public health clinics where she works in Cape Town, which since the U.S. aid cuts have been under-staffed, with fewer nurses to draw blood which is needed for viral load tests ; Said the counsellors who used to do rapid diagnostic HIV tests are also gone, and pregnant women are no longer being put on preventative HIV drugs (PrEP) because the counsellors are the ones who used to offer that ; "If all of this testing is not getting done, we don't know what level of virus pregnant women have. We don't know how many infants are acquiring HIV."

a2102.speaker: HIV experts
a2102.name: HIV experts
a2102.speech: Said that diagnostic testing was likely impacted by the funding cuts too, though that data was not available.

a2102.speaker: Sophy Moatshe, HIV activist and community leader in Diepsloot
a2102.name: Sophy Moatshe
a2102.title: HIV activist and community leader in Diepsloot
a2102.speech: Said it was hard to get HIV patients to seek care because of the stigma, and that without health workers reaching out when they miss an appointment, many fall through the cracks: "People are going to die. If there is nobody to check them, they're going to die."

a2102.speaker: Foster Mohale, spokesperson for South Africa's Department of Health
a2102.name: Foster Mohale
a2102.title: spokesperson for South Africa's Department of Health
a2102.speech: Said the government was speaking to prospective local and international donors about covering funding gaps, but declined to give details.

a2102.speaker: South African government
a2102.name: South African government
a2102.speech: Has urged HIV patients who did check-ups at the now-closed NGO-run clinics to go to public health centres instead.

a2112.speaker: Ian Khama, former President of Botswana
a2112.name: Ian Khama
a2112.title: former President of Botswana
